entries.e0f38848940b028c48b7b499639708f719d83c5d: <div sID="gen3243" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="28" osisID="Num.28" sID="Num.28"/> <div eID="gen3243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3244" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3245" type="x-p"/> Now that the people were numbered, orders given for the dividing of the land, and a general of the forces nominated and commissioned, one would have expected that the next chapter should begin the history of the campaign, or at least should give us an account of the ordinances of war; no, it contains the ordinances of worship, and provides that now, as they were on the point of entering Canaan, they should be sure to take their religion along with them, and not forget this, in the prosecution of their wars, <reference osisRef="Num.28.1-Num.28.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. The laws are here repeated and summed up concerning the sacrifices that were to be offered, I. Daily, <reference osisRef="Num.28.3-Num.28.8">ver. 3-8</reference>. II. Weekly, <reference osisRef="Num.28.9-Num.28.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. III. Monthly, <reference osisRef="Num.28.11-Num.28.15">ver. 11-15</reference>. IV. Yearly. 1. At the passover, <reference osisRef="Num.28.16-Num.28.25">ver. 16-25</reference>. 2. At pentecost, <reference osisRef="Num.28.26-Num.28.31">ver. 26-31</reference>. And the
entries.7873be2aa761f5e6d4791324568c6086b6ce5aeb: <div eID="gen3245" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3244" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Laws Concerning Sacrifices. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3246" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Command the children of Israel, and say unto them, My offering, <hi type="italic">and</hi> my bread for my sacrifices made by fire, <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sweet savour unto me, shall ye observe to offer unto me in their due season. <hi type="super">3</hi> And thou shalt say unto them, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the offering made by fire which ye shall offer unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; two lambs of the first year without spot day by day, <hi type="italic">for</hi> a continual burnt offering. <hi type="super">4</hi> The one lamb shalt thou offer in the morning, and the other lamb shalt thou offer at even; <hi type="super">5</hi> And a tenth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an ephah of flour for a meat offering, mingled with the fourth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin of beaten oil. <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> a continual burnt offering, which was ordained in Mount Sinai for a sweet savour, a sacrifice made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> And the drink offering thereof <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the fourth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin for the one lamb: in the holy <hi type="italic">place</hi> shalt thou cause the strong wine to be poured unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">for</hi> a drink offering. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the other lamb shalt thou offer at even: as the meat offering of the morning, and as the drink offering thereof, thou shalt offer <hi type="italic">it,</hi> a sacrifice made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen3246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3247" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general order given concerning the offerings of the Lord, which were to be brought in their season, <reference osisRef="Num.28.2">v. 2</reference>. These laws are here given afresh, not because the observance of them was wholly disused during their thirty-eight years' wandering in the wilderness (we cannot think that they were so long without any public worship, but that at least the daily lamb was offered morning and evening, and doubled on the sabbath day; so bishop Patrick conjectures); but that many of the sacrifices were then omitted is plainly intimated, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.25">Amos v. 25</reference>, quoted by Stephen, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.42">Acts vii. 42</reference>. <hi type="italic">Did you offer unto me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, O house of Israel?</hi> It is implied, "No, you did not." But, whether the course of sacrifices had been interrupted or no, God saw fit now to repeat the law of sacrifices, 1. Because this was a new generation of men, that were most of them unborn when the former laws were given; therefore, that they might be left without excuse, they have not only these laws written, to be read to them, but again repeated from God himself, and put into a less compass and a plainer method. 2. Because they were now entering upon war, and might be tempted to think that while they were engaged in that they should be excused from offering sacrifices. <hi type="italic">Inter arma silent leges—law is little regarded amidst the clash of arms.</hi> No, says God, <hi type="italic">my bread for my sacrifices</hi> even now <hi type="italic">shall you observe to offer,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">in the due season.</hi> They were peculiarly concerned to keep their peace with God when they were at war with their enemies. In the wilderness they were solitary, and quite separate from all other people, and therefore there they needed not so much their distinguishing badges, nor would their omission of sacrifices be so scandalous as when they came into Canaan, when they mingled with other people. 3. Because possession was now to be given them of the land of promise, that land flowing with milk and honey, where they would have plenty of all good things. "Now" (says God), "When you are feasting yourselves, forget not to offer the bread of your God." Canaan was given to them upon this condition, that they should <hi type="italic">observe God's statutes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.44-Ps.105.45">Ps. cv. 44, 45</reference>. <div eID="gen3247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3248" type="x-p"/> II. The particular law of the daily sacrifice, a lamb in the morning and a lamb in the evening, which, for the constancy of it as duly as the day came, is called a <hi type="italic">continual burnt-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.28.3">v. 3</reference>), which intimates that when we are bidden to <hi type="italic">pray always, and to pray without ceasing,</hi> it is intended that at least every morning and every evening we offer up our solemn prayers and praises to God. This is said to be <hi type="italic">ordained in Mount Sinai</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.28.6">v. 6</reference>), when the other laws were given. The institution of it we have, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38">Exod. xxix. 38</reference>. Nothing is here added in the repetition of the law, but that the wine to be poured out in the drink-offering is ordered to be <hi type="italic">strong wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.28.7">v. 7</reference>), the riches and most generous and best-bodied wine they could get. Though it was to be poured out upon the altar, and not drunk (they therefore might be ready to think the worst would serve to be so thrown away), yet God requires the strongest, to teach us to serve God with the best we have. The wine must be strong (says Ainsworth) because it was a figure of the blood of Christ, the memorial of which is still left to the church in wine, and of the blood of the martyrs, which was poured out as a drink-offering upon the <hi type="italic">sacrifice and service of our faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Phil. ii. 17</reference>.
entries.836dc14c1079953bbeb53f126c1861e28ab8e173: <div eID="gen3248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3249" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And on the sabbath day two lambs of the first year without spot, and two tenth deals of flour <hi type="italic">for</hi> a meat offering, mingled with oil, and the drink offering thereof: <hi type="super">10</hi> <hi type="italic">This is</hi> the burnt offering of every sabbath, beside the continual burnt offering, and his drink offering. <hi type="super">11</hi> And in the beginnings of your months ye shall offer a burnt offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; two young bullocks, and one ram, seven lambs of the first year without spot; <hi type="super">12</hi> And three tenth deals of flour <hi type="italic">for</hi> a meat offering, mingled with oil, for one bullock; and two tenth deals of flour <hi type="italic">for</hi> a meat offering, mingled with oil, for one ram; <hi type="super">13</hi> And a several tenth deal of flour mingled with oil <hi type="italic">for</hi> a meat offering unto one lamb; <hi type="italic">for</hi> a burnt offering of a sweet savour, a sacrifice made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> And their drink offerings shall be half an hin of wine unto a bullock, and the third <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin unto a ram, and a fourth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin unto a lamb: this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the burnt offering of every month throughout the months of the year. <hi type="super">15</hi> And one kid of the goats for a sin offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be offered, beside the continual burnt offering, and his drink offering. <div eID="gen3249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3250" type="x-p"/> The new moons and the sabbaths are often spoken of together, as great solemnities in the Jewish church, very comfortable to the saints then, and typical of gospel grace. Now we have here the sacrifices appointed, 1. For the sabbaths. Every sabbath day the offering must be doubled; besides the two lambs offered for the daily burnt-offering, there must be two more offered, one (it is probable) added to the morning sacrifice, and the other to the evening, <reference osisRef="Num.28.9-Num.28.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. This teaches us to double our devotions on sabbath days, for so the duty of the day requires. The sabbath rest is to be observed, in order to a more close application to the sabbath work, which ought to fill up sabbath time. In Ezekiel's temple-service, which points at gospel times, the sabbath offerings were to be six lambs and a ram, with their meat-offerings, and drink-offerings (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.4-Ezek.46.5">Ezek. xlvi. 4, 5</reference>), to intimate not only the continuance, but the advancement, of sabbath sanctification in the days of the Messiah. This is <hi type="italic">the burnt-offering of the sabbath in his sabbath,</hi> so it is in the original, <reference osisRef="Num.28.10">v. 10</reference>. We must do every sabbath day's work in its day, studying to redeem every minute of sabbath time as those that believe it precious; and not thinking to put off one sabbath's work to another, for sufficient to every sabbath is the service thereof. 2. For the new moons. Some suggest that, as the sabbath was kept with an eye to the creation of the world, so the new moons were sanctified with an eye to the divine providence, which <hi type="italic">appoints the moon for seasons,</hi> guiding the revolutions of time by its changes, and governing sublunary bodies (as many think) by its influences. Though we observe not any feast of new moons, yet we must not forget to give God the glory of all the precious things put forth by the moon which he has <hi type="italic">established for ever, a faithful witness in heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.37">Ps. lxxxix. 37</reference>. The offerings in the new moons were very considerable, two bullocks, a ram, and seven lambs, with the meat-offerings and drink-offerings that were to attend them (<reference osisRef="Num.28.11-Num.28.15">v. 11</reference>, &c.), besides a sin-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.28.15">v. 15</reference>. For, when we give glory to God by confessing his mercies, we must give glory to him likewise by confessing our own sins; and, when we rejoice in the gifts of common providence, we must make the sacrifice of Christ, that great gift of special grace, the fountain and spring-head of our joy. Some have questioned whether the new moons were to be reckoned among their feasts; but why should they not, when, besides the special sacrifices which were then to be offered, they rested from servile works (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Amos viii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">blew the trumpets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.10.10">ch. x. 10</reference>), and went to the prophets <hi type="italic">to hear the word?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.23">2 Kings iv. 23</reference>. And the worship performed in the new moons is made typical of gospel solemnities, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Isa. lxvi. 23</reference>.
entries.539f5624ba49537a006d05993ae1a19066fee65c: <div eID="gen3250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3251" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And in the fourteenth day of the first month <hi type="italic">is</hi> the passover of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 17 And in the fifteenth day of this month <hi type="italic">is</hi> the feast: seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten. <hi type="super">18</hi> In the first day <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> an holy convocation; ye shall do no manner of servile work <hi type="italic">therein:</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> But ye shall offer a sacrifice made by fire <hi type="italic">for</hi> a burnt offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; two young bullocks, and one ram, and seven lambs of the first year: they shall be unto you without blemish: <hi type="super">20</hi> And their meat offering <hi type="italic">shall be of</hi> flour mingled with oil: three tenth deals shall ye offer for a bullock, and two tenth deals for a ram; <hi type="super">21</hi> A several tenth deal shalt thou offer for every lamb, throughout the seven lambs: <hi type="super">22</hi> And one goat <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sin offering, to make an atonement for you. <hi type="super">23</hi> Ye shall offer these beside the burnt offering in the morning, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> for a continual burnt offering. <hi type="super">24</hi> After this manner ye shall offer daily, throughout the seven days, the meat of the sacrifice made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it shall be offered beside the continual burnt offering, and his drink offering. <hi type="super">25</hi> And on the seventh day ye shall have an holy convocation; ye shall do no servile work. <hi type="super">26</hi> Also in the day of the firstfruits, when ye bring a new meat offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , after your weeks <hi type="italic">be out,</hi> ye shall have an holy convocation; ye shall do no servile work: <hi type="super">27</hi> But ye shall offer the burnt offering for a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; two young bullocks, one ram, seven lambs of the first year; <hi type="super">28</hi> And their meat offering of flour mingled with oil, three tenth deals unto one bullock, two tenth deals unto one ram, <hi type="super">29</hi> A several tenth deal unto one lamb, throughout the seven lambs; 30 <hi type="italic">And</hi> one kid of the goats, to make an atonement for you. 31 Ye shall offer <hi type="italic">them</hi> beside the continual burnt offering, and his meat offering, (they shall be unto you without blemish) and their drink offerings. <div eID="gen3251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3252" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The appointment of the pass-over sacrifices; not that which was the chief, the paschal lamb (sufficient instructions had formerly been given concerning that), but those which were to be offered upon the seven days of unleavened bread, which followed it, <reference osisRef="Num.28.17-Num.28.25">v. 17-25</reference>. The first and last of those seven days were to be sanctified as sabbaths, by a holy rest and a holy convocation, and on each of the seven days they were to be liberal in their sacrifices, in token of their great and constant thankfulness for their deliverance out of Egypt: <hi type="italic">Two bullocks, a ram, and seven lambs.</hi> A gospel conversation, in gratitude for <hi type="italic">Christ our passover</hi> who was sacrificed, is called the <hi type="italic">keeping of this feast</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.8">1 Cor. v. 8</reference>); for it is not enough that we purge out the <hi type="italic">leavened bread</hi> of malice and wickedness, but we must <hi type="italic">offer the bread of our God, even the sacrifice of praise, continually,</hi> and continue herein unto the end. 2. The sacrifices are likewise appointed which were to be offered at the feast of pentecost, here called the <hi type="italic">day of the first-fruits,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.28.26">v. 26</reference>. In the feast of unleavened bread they offered a <hi type="italic">sheaf of their first-fruits</hi> of barley (which with them was first ripe) to the priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.10">Lev. xxiii. 10</reference>), as an introduction to the harvest; but now, about seven weeks after, they were to bring a <hi type="italic">new meat-offering to the Lord,</hi> at the end of harvest, in thankfulness to God, who had not only given, <hi type="italic">but preserved to their use, the kindly fruits of the earth, so as that in due time they did enjoy them.</hi> It was at this feast that <hi type="italic">the Spirit was poured out</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.13">Acts ii. 1</reference>, &c.), and thousands were converted by the preaching of the apostles, and were presented to Christ, to be <hi type="italic">a kind of first-fruits of his creatures.</hi> The sacrifice that was to be offered with the loaves of the first-fruits was appointed, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.18">Lev. xxiii. 18</reference>. But over and above, besides that and besides the daily offerings, they were to offer <hi type="italic">two bullocks, one ram, and seven lambs, with a kid for a sin-offering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.28.27-Num.28.30">v. 27-30</reference>. When God sows plentifully upon us he expects to reap accordingly from us. Bishop Patrick observes that no <hi type="italic">peace-offerings</hi> are appointed in this chapter, which were chiefly for the benefit of the offerers, and therefore in them they were left more to themselves; but <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings</hi> were purely for the honour of God, were confessions of his dominion, and typified evangelical piety and devotion, by which the soul is wholly offered up to God in the flames of holy love; and <hi type="italic">sin-offerings</hi> were typical of Christ's sacrifice of himself, <hi type="italic">by which we and our services are perfected and sanctified.</hi>  <chapter eID="Num.28"/> <div eID="gen3252" type="x-p"/>

entries.9696d11c87a226d6a6a2255266e6b6e672386787: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1565"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 28</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.28.1-Num.28.31">Nu 28:1-31</reference>. Offerings to Be Observed.</title> <div sID="gen2101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1565"/><hi type="bold">2. Command the children of Israel, and say unto them--</hi>The repetition of several laws formerly enacted, which is made in this chapter, was seasonable and necessary, not only on account of their importance and the frequent neglect of them, but because a new generation had sprung up since their first institution and because the Israelites were about to be settled in the land where those ordinances were to be observed.<div eID="gen2101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">My offering, and my bread--</hi>used generally for the appointed offerings, and the import of the prescription is to enforce regularity and care in their observance. <div eID="gen2102" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca3cb4843b551950b2d51b839a92d7558c0d11d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1566"/><div sID="gen2103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1566"/><hi type="bold">9-10. This is the burnt offering of every sabbath--</hi>There is no previous mention of a Sabbath burnt offering, which was additional to the daily sacrifices. <div eID="gen2103" type="x-p"/>
entries.da4d150dc7010fa669afc9c320f4a58de4e51d61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1567"/><div sID="gen2104" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1567"/><hi type="bold">11-15. And in the beginnings of your months ye shall offer a burnt offering unto the Lord--</hi>These were held as sacred festivals; and though not possessing the character of solemn feasts, they were distinguished by the blowing of trumpets over the sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Num.10.10">Nu 10:10</reference>), by the suspension of all labor except the domestic occupations of women (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Am 8:5</reference>), by the celebration of public worship (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.23">2Ki 4:23</reference>), and by social or family feasts (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.5">1Sa 20:5</reference>). These observations are not prescribed in the law though they obtained in the practice of a later time. The beginning of the month was known, not by astronomical calculations, but, according to Jewish writers, by the testimony of messengers appointed to watch the first visible appearance of the new moon; and then the fact was announced through the whole country by signal-fires kindled on the mountain tops. The new-moon festivals having been common among the heathen, it is probable that an important design of their institution in Israel was to give the minds of that people a better direction; and assuming this to have been one of the objects contemplated, it will account for one of the kids being offered unto the Lord (<reference osisRef="Num.28.15">Nu 28:15</reference>), not unto the moon, as the Egyptians and Syrians did. The Sabbath and the new moon are frequently mentioned together. <div eID="gen2104" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b5eaf0be0d80540be10cb054722068afa806e59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1568"/><div sID="gen2105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1568"/><hi type="bold">16-25. in the fourteenth day of the first month is the passover--</hi>The law for that great annual festival is given (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.5">Le 23:5</reference>), but some details are here introduced, as certain specified offerings are prescribed to be made on each of the seven days of unleavened bread [Nu 28:18-25]. <div eID="gen2105" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c891ac52044028e42a8304d5316c223d51207cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1569"/><div sID="gen2106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1569"/><hi type="bold">26-27. in the day of the first-fruits ... offer the burnt offering--</hi>A new sacrifice is here ordered for the celebration of this festival, in addition to the other offering, which was to accompany the first-fruits (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.18">Le 23:18</reference>). <chapter eID="Num.28"/>

entries.8314afafef71e7dec6dda12bab3dffcce855f0d6: <div eID="gen6094" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6095" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6096" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6096" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6095" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6097" type="x-p"/> All the offerings of God to be offered in their due season, <reference osisRef="Num.28.1">Num 28:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.2">Num 28:2</reference>. The continual burnt-offering for the morning, <reference osisRef="Num.28.3-Num.28.6">Num 28:3-6</reference>; and its drink-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.28.7">Num 28:7</reference>. The continual burnt-offering for the evening, <reference osisRef="Num.28.8">Num 28:8</reference>. The offerings for the Sabbath, <reference osisRef="Num.28.9">Num 28:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.10">Num 28:10</reference>. The offerings for the beginning of each month, <reference osisRef="Num.28.11-Num.28.15">Num 28:11-15</reference>. Repetition of the ordinances concerning the passover, <reference osisRef="Num.28.16-Num.28.25">Num 28:16-25</reference>. Ordinances concerning the day of first-fruits or pentecost, <reference osisRef="Num.28.26-Num.28.31">Num 28:26-31</reference>.
entries.58aa6b45cd9157d94bec1e0ebfbab2600f9a6df1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen6097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6098" type="x-p"/> Command the children of Israel, etc. - It is not easy to account for the reason of the introduction of these precepts here, which had been so circumstantially delivered before in different parts of the books of Exodus and Leviticus. It is possible that the daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly services had been considerably interrupted for several years, owing to the unsettled state of the people in the wilderness, and that it was necessary to repeat these laws for two reasons: <div eID="gen6098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6099" type="x-p"/> 1. Because they were now about to enter into the promised land, where these services must be established and constant. <div eID="gen6099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6100" type="x-p"/> 2. Because the former generations being all dead, multitudes of the present might be ignorant of these ordinances. <div eID="gen6100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6101" type="x-p"/> In their due season - Moses divides these offerings into: - <div eID="gen6101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6102" type="x-p"/> 1. Daily. The morning and evening sacrifices: a lamb each time, <reference osisRef="Num.28.3">Num 28:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.4">Num 28:4</reference>. <div eID="gen6102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6103" type="x-p"/> 2. Weekly. The Sabbath offerings, two lambs of a year old, <reference osisRef="Num.28.9">Num 28:9</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen6103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6104" type="x-p"/> 3. Monthly. At the beginning of each month two young bullocks, one ram, and seven lambs of a year old, and a kid for a sin-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.28.11">Num 28:11</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen6104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6105" type="x-p"/> 4. Annual.1. The passover to last seven days; the offerings, two young bullocks, one ram, seven lambs of a year old, and a he-goat for a sin-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.28.16">Num 28:16</reference>, etc. 2. The day of First-Fruits. The sacrifices, the same as on the beginning of the month, <reference osisRef="Num.28.26">Num 28:26</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen6105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6106" type="x-p"/> With these sacrifices were offered libations, or drink-offerings of strong wine, <reference osisRef="Num.28.7">Num 28:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.14">Num 28:14</reference>, and minchahs, or meat-offerings, composed of fine flour mingled with oil, <reference osisRef="Num.28.8">Num 28:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.12">Num 28:12</reference>, etc. For an ample account of all these offerings, see the notes on Leviticus 7 (note) and Exodus 12 (note).
entries.1504f917ee65b3be3f2e9f8458628b6dc49f7b5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen6106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6107" type="x-p"/> Strong wine - Sikera; see the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.10.9">Lev 10:9</reference>, where this is largely explained.

entries.56e3288727aac58a074ec673ec40bc6f4e3a418f: Num 28:1 <div eID="gen2011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2012" type="x-p"/> When Israel was prepared for the conquest of the promised land by the fresh numbering and mustering of its men, and by the appointment of Joshua as commander, its relation to the Lord was regulated by a law which determined the sacrifices through which it was to maintain its fellowship with its God from day to day, and serve Him as His people (Num 28 and 29). Through this order of sacrifice, the object of which was to form and sanctify the whole life of the congregation into a continuous worship, the sacrificial and festal laws already given in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.14-Exod.23.17">Exo 23:14-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.42">Exo 29:38-42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.31.12-Exod.31.17">Exo 31:12-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.1">Lev 23:1</reference>, and Num 25:1-12, were completed and arranged into a united and well-ordered whole. “It was very fitting that this law should be issued a short time before the advance into Canaan; for it was there first that the Israelites were in a position to carry out the sacrificial worship in all its full extent, and to observe all the sacrificial and festal laws” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). The law commences with the daily morning and evening burnt-offering (Num 28:3-8), which was instituted at Sinai at the dedication of the altar. It is not merely for the sake of completeness that it is introduced here, or for the purpose of including all the national sacrifices that were to be offered during the whole year in one general survey; but also for an internal reason, viz., that the daily sacrifice was also to be offered on the Sabbaths and feast-days, to accompany the general and special festal sacrifices, and to form the common substratum for the whole of these. Then follow in Num 28:9-15 the sacrifices to be offered on the Sabbath and at the new moon; and in Num 28:16 - Num 29:38 the general sacrifices for the different yearly feasts, which were to be added to the sacrifices that were peculiar to each particular festival, having been appointed at the time of its first institution, and being specially adapted to give expression to its specific character, so that, at the yearly feasts, the congregation had to offer their different kinds of sacrifices: (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) the daily morning and evening sacrifice; (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) the general sacrifices that were offered on every feast-day; and (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) the festal sacrifices that were peculiar to each particular feast. This cumulative arrangement is to be explained from the significance of the daily and of the festal sacrifices. In the daily burnt-offering the congregation of Israel, as a congregation of Jehovah, was to sanctify its life, body, soul, and spirit, to the Lord its God; and on the Lord’s feast-days it was to give expression to this sanctification in an intensified form. This stronger practical exhibition of the sanctification of the life was embodied in the worship by the elevation and graduation of the daily sacrifice, through the addition of a second and much more considerable burnt-offering, meat-offering, and drink-offering. The graduation was regulated by the significance of the festivals. On the Sabbaths the daily sacrifice was doubled, by the presentation of a burnt-offering consisting of two lambs. On the other feast-days it was increased by a burnt-offering composed of oxen, rams, and yearling lambs, which was always preceded by a sin-offering. - As the seventh day of the week, being a Sabbath, was distinguished above the other days of the week, as a day that was sanctified to the Lord in a higher degree than the rest, by an enlarged burnt-offering, meat-offering, and drink-offering; so the seventh month, being a Sabbath-month, was raised above the other months of the year, and sanctified as a festal month, by the fact that, in addition to the ordinary new moon sacrifices of two bullocks, one ram, and seven yearling lambs, a special festal sacrifice was also offered, consisting of one bullock, one ram, and seven yearling lambs (Num 29:2), which was also repeated on the day of atonement, and at the close of the feast of Tabernacles (Num 29:8, Num 29:36); and also that the feast of Tabernacles, which fell in this month, was to be celebrated by a much larger number of burnt-offerings, as the largest and holiest feast of the congregation of Israel.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> remarks as to the difference in the sacrifices are not only erroneous, but likely to mislead, and tending to obscure and distort the actual facts. “On those feast-days,” he says, “which were intended as a general festival to Jehovah, viz., the sabbatical portion of the seventh new moon, the day of atonement, and the closing day of the yearly feasts, the sacrifices consisted of one bullock, one ram, and seven yearling lambs (Num 29:2, Num 29:8, Num 29:36); whereas at the older festivals which had a reference to nature, such as the new moons, the days of unleavened bread, and the feast of Weeks, they consisted of two bullocks, one ram, and seven yearling lambs (Num 28:11, Num 28:19, Num 28:24, Num 28:27; Num 29:6), and at the feast of Tabernacles of even a larger number, especially of bullocks (Num 29:12.). In the last, Jehovah was especially honoured, as having poured out His blessing upon nature, and granted a plentiful harvest to the cultivation of the soil. The ox was the beast of agriculture.” It was not the so-called “older festivals which had reference to nature” that were distinguished by a larger number of sacrificial animals, above those feast-days which were intended as general festivals to Jehovah, but the feasts of the seventh month alone. Thus the seventh new moon’s day was celebrated by a double new moon’s sacrifice, viz., with three bullocks, two rams, and fourteen yearling lambs; the feast of atonement, as the introductory festival of the feast of Tabernacles, by a special festal sacrifice, whilst the day of Passover, which corresponded to it in the first festal cycle, as the introductory festival of the feast of unleavened bread, had no general festal sacrifices; and, lastly, the feast of Tabernacles, not only by a very considerable increase in the number of the festal sacrifices on every one of the seven days, but also by the addition of an eighth day, as the octave of the feast, and a festal sacrifice answering to those of the first and seventh days of this month.</note> <div eID="gen2012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2013" type="x-p"/> All the feasts of the whole year, for example, formed a cycle of feast-days, arranged according to the number seven, which had its starting-point and centre in the Sabbath, and was regulated according to the division of time established at the creation, into weeks, months, years, and periods of years, ascending from the weekly Sabbath to the monthly Sabbath, the sabbatical year, and the year of jubilee. In this cycle of holy periods, regulated as it was by the number seven, and ever expanding into larger and larger circles, there was embodied the whole revolution of annually recurring festivals, established to commemorate the mighty works of the Lord for the preservation and inspiration of His people. And this was done in the following manner: in the <hi type="italic">first</hi> place, the number of yearly feasts amounted to exactly seven, of which the two leading feasts (<hi type="italic">Mazzoth</hi> and the feast of <hi type="italic">Tabernacles</hi>) lasted <hi type="italic">seven</hi> days; in the <hi type="italic">second</hi> place, in all the feasts, some of which were of only one day’s duration, whilst others lasted seven days, there were only <hi type="italic">seven</hi> days that were to be observed with sabbatical rest and a holy meeting; and in the <hi type="italic">third</hi> place, the seven feasts were formed into two large festal circles, each of which consisted of an introductory feast, the main feast of <hi type="italic">seven</hi> days, and a closing feast of one day. The <hi type="italic">first</hi> of these festal circles was commemorative of the elevation of Israel into the nation of God, and its subsequent preservation. It commenced on the 14th Abib (Nisan) with the Passover, which was appointed to commemorate the deliverance of Israel from the destroying angel who smote the first-born of Egypt, as the introductory festival. It culminated in the <hi type="italic">seven</hi> days’ feast of unleavened bread, as the feast of the deliverance of Israel from bondage, and its elevation into the nation of God; and closed with the feast of Weeks, Pentecost, or the feast of Harvest, which was kept <hi type="italic">seven</hi> weeks after the offering of the sheaf of first-fruits, on the second day of Mazzoth. This festal circle contained only three days that were to be kept with sabbatical rest and a holy meeting (viz., the first and seventh days of Mazzoth and the day of Pentecost). The <hi type="italic">second</hi> festal circle fell entirely in the seventh month, and its main object was to inspire the Israelites in their enjoyment of the blessings of their God: for this reason it was celebrated by the presentation of a large number of burnt-offerings. This festal circle opened with the day of atonement, which was appointed for the tenth day of the seventh month, as the introductory feast, culminated in the <hi type="italic">seven days'</hi> feast of Tabernacles, and closed with the eighth day, which was added to the seven feast-days as the octave of this festive circle, or the solemn close of all the feasts of the year. This also included only three days that were to be commemorated with sabbatical rest and a holy meeting (the 10th, 15th, and 22nd of the month); but to these we have to add the day of trumpets, with which the month commenced, which was also a Sabbath of rest with a holy meeting; and this completes the seven days of rest (see my <hi type="italic">Archaeologie</hi>, i. §76). <div eID="gen2013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2014" type="x-p"/> Num 28:2 contains the general instruction to offer to the Lord His sacrificial gift “at the time appointed by Him.” On <hi type="italic">corban</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Lev.1.2">Lev 1:2</reference>; on “<hi type="italic">the bread of Jehovah</hi>,” at <reference osisRef="Lev.3.11">Lev 3:11</reference>; on the “<hi type="italic">sacrifice made by fire</hi>,” and “<hi type="italic">a sweet savour</hi>,” at <reference osisRef="Lev.1.9">Lev 1:9</reference>; and on “<hi type="italic">moed</hi>,” at <reference osisRef="Lev.23.2">Lev 23:2</reference>, Lev 23:4.
entries.42c9cedf7600dfbcb67aae4ae123d5d60a2c1ecc: Num 28:3-6 <div eID="gen2014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2015" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">The daily sacrifice: </hi>as it had already been instituted at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.42">Exo 29:38-42</reference>).
entries.03632083c5c9238639d97d52a58e7730c17ae27a: Num 28:7-8 <div eID="gen2015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2016" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">In the sanctuary</hi>,” i.e., περὶ τὸν βωμόν (round about the altar), as <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> paraphrases it (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. iii. 10); not “with (in) holy vessels,” as <hi type="italic">Jonathan</hi> and others interpret it. “<hi type="italic">Pour out a drink-offering, as</hi> שׁכר <hi type="italic">for Jehovah</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Shecar</hi> does not mean intoxicating drink here (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.10.9">Lev 10:9</reference>), but <hi type="italic">strong drink</hi>, in distinction from water as simple drink. The drink-offering consisted of wine only (see at Num 15:5.); and hence <hi type="italic">Onkelos</hi> paraphrases it, “of old wine.”
entries.6bb0d017e1daa0b3279158a55b266827b06a0b79: Num 28:9-10 <div eID="gen2016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2017" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Sabbath-offering</hi>, which was to be added to the daily sacrifice (על, upon it), consisted of two yearling lambs as a burnt-offering, with the corresponding meat-offering and drink-offering, according to the general rule laid down in Num 15:3., and is appointed here for the first time; whereas the sabbatical feast had already been instituted at <reference osisRef="Exod.20.8-Exod.20.11">Exo 20:8-11</reference> and Lev 23:3. “<hi type="italic">The burnt-offering of the Sabbath on its Sabbath</hi>,” i.e., as often as the Sabbath occurred, every Sabbath.
entries.1c1e151db48741fe04f64d89edd5fba703695203: Num 28:11-15 <div eID="gen2017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2018" type="x-p"/> At the beginnings of the month, i.e., at the <hi type="italic">new moons</hi>, a larger burnt-offering was to be added to the daily or continual burnt-offering, consisting of two bullocks (young oxen), one ram, and seven yearling lambs, with the corresponding meat and drink-offerings, as the “month’s burnt-offering in its (i.e., every) month with regard to the months of the year,” i.e., corresponding to them. To this there was also to be added a sin-offering of a shaggy goat (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.4.23">Lev 4:23</reference>). The custom of distinguishing the beginnings of the months of new moon’s days by a peculiar festal sacrifice, without their being, strictly speaking, festal days, with sabbatical rest and a holy meeting,<note placement="foot">In later times, however, the new moon grew more and more into a feast-day, trade was suspended (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Amo 8:5</reference>), the pious Israelite sought instruction from the prophets (2Ki 4:23), many families and households presented yearly thank-offerings (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.6">1Sa 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.29">1Sa 20:29</reference>), and at a still later period the most devout abstained from fasting (Judith 8:6); consequently it is frequently referred to by the prophets as a feast resembling the Sabbath (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference>; Hos 2:13; <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1">Eze 46:1</reference>).</note> arose from the relation in which the month stood to the single day. “If the congregation was to sanctify its life and labour to the Lord every day by a burnt-offering, it could not well be omitted at the commencement of the larger division of time formed by the month; on the contrary, it was only right that the commencement of a new month should be sanctified by a special sacrifice. Whilst, then, a burnt-offering, in which the idea of expiation was subordinate to that of consecrating surrender to the Lord, was sufficient for the single day; for the whole month it was necessary that, in consideration of the sins that had been committed in the course of the past month, and had remained without expiation, a special sin-offering should be offered for their expiation, in order that, upon the ground of the forgiveness and reconciliation with God which had been thereby obtained, the lives of the people might be sanctified afresh to the Lord in the burnt-offering. This significance of the new moon sacrifice was still further intensified by the fact, that during the presentation of the sacrifice the priests sounded the silver trumpets, in order that it might be to the congregation for a memorial before God (Num 10:10). The trumpet blast was intended to bring before God the prayers of the congregation embodied in the sacrifice, that God might remember them in mercy, granting them the forgiveness of their sins and power for sanctification, and quickening them again in the fellowship of His saving grace” (see my <hi type="italic">Archaeologie</hi>, i. p. 369).
entries.f73b357855b0a127f436647e0b25b557a0a1c409: Num 28:16-22 <div eID="gen2018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2019" type="x-p"/> The same number of sacrifices as at the new moon were to be offered on every one of the seven days of the feast of unleavened bread (<hi type="italic">Mazzoth</hi>), from the 15th to the 21st of the month, whereas there was no general festal offering on the day of the Passover, or the 14th of the month (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.3-Exod.12.14">Exo 12:3-14</reference>). With regard to the feast of <hi type="italic">Mazzoth</hi>, the rule is repeated from <reference osisRef="Exod.12.15-Exod.12.20">Exo 12:15-20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.23.6-Lev.23.8">Lev 23:6-8</reference>, that on the first and seventh day there was to be a Sabbath rest and holy meeting.
entries.50452a3090734fb08514ea7aaf87beff32bb9108: Num 28:23-25 <div eID="gen2019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2020" type="x-p"/> The festal sacrifices of the seven days were to be prepared “in addition to the morning burnt-offering, which served as the continual burnt-offering.” This implies that the festal sacrifices commanded were to be prepared and offered every day after the morning sacrifice.
entries.ba39d8385374e817f6aebb4c53c05b787628ab03: Num 28:26-31 <div eID="gen2020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2021" type="x-p"/> The same number of sacrifices is appointed for the day of the first-fruits, i.e., for the <hi type="italic">feast of Weeks</hi> or <hi type="italic">Harvest feast</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.23.15-Lev.23.22">Lev 23:15-22</reference>). The festal burnt-offering and sin-offering of this one day was independent of the supplementary burnt-offering and sin-offering of the wave-loaves appointed in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.18">Lev 23:18</reference>, and was to be offered before these and after the daily morning sacrifice.  <chapter eID="Num.28"/> <div eID="gen2021" type="x-p"/>

entries.a21fed47b34fb99b1b44eb90be607547dc01744b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.28.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.28.1" sID="gen12577" type="section"/> <div sID="gen12578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the Lord spake unto Moses.</hi> Moses, being about to speak again of the “continual” sacrifice, premises in general that the people should diligently follow in their offerings whatever God has enjoined; for by the word “observe,” (<hi type="italic">custodiendi,</hi>) not only diligence, but obedience is also expressed. But, in order that they should more earnestly beware of every transgression, God calls either that which was wont daily to be placed on the table, or that which was annexed to the burnt-offerings, <hi type="italic">His </hi>bread, as if He ate of it after the manner of men. It is indeed a hard expression, but the rudeness of His ancient people obliged Him to speak thus grossly, that, on the one hand, they might learn this rite to be acceptable to God, just as food is acceptable to man; and, on the other, that they might study to offer their sacrifices more purely and chastely.<div eID="gen12578" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.28.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen12577" osisID="Num.28.1" type="section"/>
entries.8e7edf7f733755fe4fc38b06a68c3897916439ae: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.28.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.28.3" sID="gen12579" type="section"/> <div sID="gen12580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">And thou shalt say unto them.</hi> He repeats what we have seen in Exodus, that they should kill two lambs daily, one in the morning, and the other in the evening; but he speaks more fully of the concomitants of flour and wine, and also refers to the antiquity of this kind of sacrifice as its recommendation, because it began to be offered to God on Mount Sinai, and was a “savor of rest.” <note n="236"> <div sID="gen12581" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">A.V.,</hi> “a sweet savor.” <hi type="italic">Margin, “Heb., </hi>a savor of my rest."<div eID="gen12581" type="x-p"/> </note> The libation of wine, of which mention is made, was also in use among heathen nations; but, inasmuch as it was without the command and promise of God, it could not but be unmeaning (<foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">insipidum</hi></foreign> ) <note n="237"> <div sID="gen12582" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fr., “</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr">c’a este moins que ripopper, comme on dit</foreign>;” <hi type="italic">Ripope, </hi>i.e.,bad wine.<div eID="gen12582" type="x-p"/> </note> And it is probable (as we have seen elsewhere) that many of the heathen rites descended from the ancient fathers but as a false and empty imitation; for when they had forgotten the reason of them, all they did could only be a mere theatrical pageantry. But we have said that thus men were reminded always to have God before their eyes in their daily food; and therefore in every way to accustom themselves to cultivate holiness.<div eID="gen12580" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.28.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen12579" osisID="Num.28.3" type="section"/>

9. And on the Sabbath-day. What was omitted in the former passage is here supplied, i.e., that on the Sabbath the continual sacrifice was to be doubled, and two lambs offered instead of one; for it was reasonable that, as the seventh day was peculiarly dedicated to God, it should be exalted above other days by some extraordinary and distinctive mark. He also commands greater sacrifices to be offered at the beginning of the month or new moon, viz., two bullocks and one ram, and a goat for a sin-offering; for we know that the first day of every month was consecrated to God, that the people might more frequently have the remembrance of their religious duties renewed; and the goat for an atonement for sin was added, in order that every month they should present themselves as guilty before God to deprecate His wrath.

entries.e53fbc25e53ea6485de928581bc9a0f41c84951c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.28.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.28.16" sID="gen12621" type="section"/> <div sID="gen12622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> <hi type="italic">And in the fourteenth day.</hi> It is true that the instruction here given has some connection with the feast of the passover, but since the sacrifices are avowedly treated of, and no mention is made of its other observances, except in this place, I have connected it with the continual sacrifice, as its concomitant or part. Moses cursorily refers, indeed, to what we have already seen, <hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>that the people should abstain from leaven for seven days, and eat unleavened bread; but he afterwards descends to the main point of which he here proposed to treat, viz., that the people should slay two bullocks as a burnt-offering, a ram, and seven lambs, together with a goat for a sin-offering; and that this sacrifice should be repeated through the whole week. In order, then, that the reverence paid to the passover should be increased, this extraordinary sacrifice was added to the continual one, partly that they might thus be more and more stimulated to devote themselves to God; partly that they might acknowledge how familiarly He had embraced them with His favor, inasmuch as He took these offerings from their flocks and herds, and required the sacred feast to be prepared for Him out of their cellars and granaries also; partly, too, that professing themselves to be worthy of eternal death, they should fly to Him to ask for pardon, and at the same time should understand that there was but one way of reconciliation, <hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>when God should be propitiated by sacrifice.<div eID="gen12622" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.28.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen12621" osisID="Num.28.16" type="section"/>

Then, also, he instructs them, the continual sacrifice was to be increased by the addition of two bullocks, one ram, seven lambs, a goat for a sin-offering, together with the <hi type="italic">minha </hi>and a libation, with the object, of which I have already spoken. A perplexing difficulty here arises, because in <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.23">Leviticus 23</reference>, one bullock is mentioned instead of two, and, on the contrary, two rams instead of one. <note n="238"> <div sID="gen12625" type="x-p"/> “Josephus and Maimonides understand that they were distinct sacrifices. Aben-Ezra and others think that it was left to the priest which he would offer.” — Brightwell on the Pentateuch, <hi type="italic">in loco</hi>.<div eID="gen12625" type="x-p"/> </note> Some think that an option was left to the priests in this matter; but when I consider how precisely God’s commands were given in everything, I question whether such an alternative was left to their discretion. The notion that God had once been content with a single bullock, as some think, because they were not abundant in the desert, appears to me a subterfuge. I confess I do not know how to get out of this difficulty, unless perhaps we say, that inasmuch as sufficiently exact provision had been made, in all other particulars, that nothing should be done without reason, in this respect only they were reminded that God in Himself cares not for greater or less victims. Nor does any reverence prevent us from saying that, as it sometimes happens in minor matters, a wrong number may have crept in from the carelessness of scribes; <note n="239"> <div sID="gen12626" type="x-p"/> The conjecture of <hi type="italic">C.</hi> receives no support from the modern collections of various readings; for though the number <hi type="italic">two </hi>is wanting in one of Kennicott’s <hi type="italic">MSS., </hi>the word for bullocks is in the plural in that same <hi type="italic">MS.; </hi>and the two most ancient versions, viz., the <hi type="italic">LXX. </hi>and the <hi type="italic">Syriac </hi>agree with the received text both here and in <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.8">Leviticus 23:8</reference>. — <hi type="italic">W.</hi><div eID="gen12626" type="x-p"/> </note> and this is probably the most natural solution. The more correct reading, in my opinion, is, that they should offer two bullocks and one ram; but since it is elsewhere explained why God appointed this day, he only briefly recites here: “When they
